source.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
source.authors: Valérie Costa; Thomas Fel; E. Lubana; Bahareh Tolooshams; Demba E. Ba

page_placements.theme: SAE architectures that build in a hierarchy

record.tranche_reason: The study compares SAE variants on controlled hierarchical synthetic data and reports feature absorption and hierarchy recovery. This bears on the absorption and objective-dependence challenge versions, but it does not test dictionary-size-driven splitting.
record.gate_note: No results compare increasing dictionary sizes or track whether smaller-dictionary features are partitioned into larger-dictionary features. The study does not test whether a coarse feature's inputs are covered by child features across dictionary sizes. Its synthetic hierarchy and learned-dictionary results are reported here; cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: On a controlled synthetic parent–child hierarchy, the study measures feature absorption in Vanilla, BatchTopK, Matryoshka and MP-SAE. It also argues that the original benchmark's perfectly correlated firing magnitudes favour absorption. This bears on V4 (absorption occurs) and V6 (it depends on the objective and inputs). There is no dictionary-size sweep, so V1, V2, V3 and V5 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that standard SAEs, and also Matryoshka despite its hierarchical objective, fail to faithfully capture conditionally orthogonal hierarchical features: Vanilla and BatchTopK show absorption. MP-SAE recovers hierarchy at low to moderate interference and favours hierarchy over flat structure at high interference. It also recovers multimodal features in VLMs. They argue this shows the limits of assuming purely linear structure.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce dictionary-size-driven feature splitting. It trains and compares SAE architectures on synthetic hierarchical data with controlled within-level correlations, including MP-SAE, and evaluates learned feature geometry and activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with SAE architecture and within-level correlation (0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9). The paper also reports that Matryoshka mitigation varies across runs and that MP-SAE behavior under perfectly correlated firings can be unstable.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE architectures differ in recovering within-level (flat) correlations versus cross-level (hierarchical) separation: Flat MSE and Hierarchical MSE in Fig. 4, with high-correlation degradation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE inductive biases trade off recovery of within-level concept correlation against preservation of hierarchical separation.

record.problems: The absorption evidence is primarily qualitative in the reported text and figures. The synthetic experiments use a controlled two-level hierarchy, and the study does not test dictionary-size variation or whether features partition a coarse feature's inputs. Some Matryoshka outcomes are described as inconsistent; high within-level correlation degrades recovery for all architectures.

untested.parts: All of it: no dictionary-size sweep, cross-size matching or input-partition test.
All of it: no size-dependent splitting in large models or across open SAE releases.
All of it: no nested families of split features. Conditional orthogonality concerns ground-truth and learned dictionaries, not split families.
Whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes absorption: all SAEs use a fixed ℓ0 target of 1.36 and one width.
All of it: no cross-size decomposition and no test for novel latents.
Whether splitting says little about pretrained models' own units: absorption is measured only in the synthetic setting. Matryoshka is not tested on size-driven splitting.

missing.what: Absorption scores (cosine of child feature to parent) for MP, Matryoshka, Vanilla and BatchTopK across child firing means and variances. Vanilla ≈0.45–0.70, BatchTopK ≈0.42–0.54, Matryoshka ≈0.05–0.22, MP ≈0.001–0.07.
Original Matryoshka benchmark with perfectly correlated firings: Vanilla consistently absorbs, Matryoshka avoids absorption with negative interference, MP-SAE unstable.
Quantitative Flat MSE and Hierarchical MSE across within-level correlation levels (median of 10 runs).

record.verdict_notes: The main text (Fig. 4A) says Matryoshka 'avoids absorption', while Appendix B.1.3 says it only occasionally does; the verdict follows the appendix. The study is not an original source. No row bears on V1, V2, V3 or V5. The VLM split-dictionary (modality) finding concerns modality-specific features, not dictionary-size splitting, and is not recorded.

versions.untested_parts: No dictionary-size sweep, cross-size feature matching, input-partition test, or comparison of directions across dictionary sizes.
Although the paper uses vision, vision-language, and preliminary language-model settings, it does not test the claimed size-dependent splitting pattern across large models or SAE releases.
The paper tests hierarchical recovery and conditional orthogonality, not nested families of split features that are geometrically close and mirror a concept hierarchy.

The study reports parent-child feature absorption and its mitigation, but does not directly test whether a parent latent fails to fire exactly where a child takes over. It does not vary SAE dictionary size or sparsity to test whether those changes fix absorption.
No cross-size decomposition of larger latents into smaller latents, or test for novel latents across dictionary sizes.

The study compares architectures/objectives on synthetic hierarchical data and reports differences in absorption and hierarchy recovery. It does not establish that splitting is an artifact that says little about units in pretrained models, or test Matryoshka SAEs on dictionary-size splitting.

rows.subject: Vanilla (ReLU) SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data with controlled within-level correlation; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Parent-child feature absorption and recovery of hierarchical structure.
rows.value: Child features are often aligned with their parent features; when a child is active, parent activation values are underestimated. The ground-truth active set is correctly identified.
rows.note: The paper describes absorption, but does not report exact parent-latent non-firing where a child activates.
rows.check: Linking is correct. Absorption is shown as child features aligned with parents and parent activations underestimated, not as parent non-firing.

rows.subject: BatchTopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data with controlled within-level correlation; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Parent-child feature absorption and recovery of hierarchical structure.
rows.value: Child features are often aligned with their parent features; when a child is active, parent activation values are underestimated. The ground-truth active set is correctly identified.
rows.note: The paper describes absorption, but does not report exact parent-latent non-firing where a child activates.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained with a hierarchical reconstruction objective on synthetic hierarchical data; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Parent-child absorption and preservation of within-level correlations.
rows.value: It sometimes mitigates absorption, but introduces negative correlations between same-level features and can partially misalign them; some runs fail.
rows.note: Mitigation is inconsistent and comes with distortion of the flat, within-level structure.

source_check.problem: Sec 4.1 main text says Matryoshka avoids absorption, while the appendix says only occasionally (failed runs in rows 2 and 4). Partial is right.

rows.subject: MP-SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data using residual-guided Matching Pursuit inference; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Parent-child absorption and recovery of the ground-truth dictionary and sparse codes.
rows.value: Perfectly recovers the ground-truth dictionary and sparse codes, with no feature absorption.
rows.note: This is an alternative architecture, not a change in dictionary size or sparsity.
rows.check: Absorption is absent under MP-SAE. For V6 this absence is the predicted objective-driven reduction, not a failure. MP-SAE is an architecture change, not a size or sparsity change.

source_check.problem: MP-SAE uses tied weights and no fixed l0 target (B.1.2).

rows.subject: Vanilla (ReLU) SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data with controlled within-level correlation; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Parent-child feature absorption and recovery of hierarchical structure.
rows.value: Feature absorption remains a consistent issue; the model partially reflects ground-truth correlations among parent nodes without children.
rows.note: Absorption is reported alongside partial recovery of some within-level correlations.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained with a hierarchical reconstruction objective on synthetic hierarchical data; evaluated learned features and activations.

rows.subject: MP-SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data using residual-guided Matching Pursuit inference; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Parent-child absorption and recovery of sparse codes and hierarchical structure.
rows.value: Maintains perfect recovery, with inferred sparse codes matching the ground truth and no evidence of feature absorption.
rows.note: This is an alternative architecture, not a change in dictionary size or sparsity.

rows.subject: Vanilla (ReLU) SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data with controlled within-level correlation; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Recovery of within-level correlations and hierarchical organization.
rows.value: Partially captures within-level correlations, with the closest correlation values among child nodes; correlations are weaker or less accurate for other node types.
rows.note: The paper does not separately state an absorption outcome for this setting.
rows.check: Measures recovery of within-level correlation, not absorption or splitting. No absorption outcome is stated for this setting.

rows.subject: BatchTopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data with controlled within-level correlation; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Recovery of within-level correlations and hierarchical organization.
rows.value: Partially captures within-level correlations, with the closest correlation values among child nodes; correlations are weaker or less accurate for other node types.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained with a hierarchical reconstruction objective on synthetic hierarchical data; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Recovery of within-level dependencies and hierarchical organization.
rows.value: Fails to recover meaningful within-level dependencies.
rows.note: The paper says MP-SAE preserves the hierarchical organization more faithfully in this setting.
rows.check: Measures within-level dependency recovery, not absorption.

rows.subject: MP-SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data using residual-guided Matching Pursuit inference; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Recovery of within-level correlations and hierarchical organization.
rows.value: Partially recovers within-level correlations, particularly among parent nodes without children, and more faithfully preserves hierarchical organization.
rows.note: The paper reports partial, not complete, recovery of the ground-truth correlations.
rows.check: Measures within-level correlation and hierarchy preservation, not absorption.

rows.subject: Vanilla (ReLU) SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data with controlled within-level correlation; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Recovery of hierarchy and within-level correlations.
rows.value: Performance degrades; it captures some similarity among last-layer children but tends to flatten the hierarchy by focusing on correlated low-level features and neglecting higher-level ones.
rows.note: The high-correlation setting changes the outcome relative to lower-correlation settings.
rows.check: Measures hierarchy flattening and correlation recovery under high interference, not absorption specifically.

rows.subject: BatchTopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data with controlled within-level correlation; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Recovery of hierarchy and within-level correlations.
rows.value: Performance degrades; it captures some similarity among last-layer children but tends to flatten the hierarchy by focusing on correlated low-level features and neglecting higher-level ones.
rows.note: The high-correlation setting changes the outcome relative to lower-correlation settings.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained with a hierarchical reconstruction objective on synthetic hierarchical data; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Recovery of hierarchy and within-level correlations.
rows.value: Performance degrades in the high-correlation setting; the study reports that all SAEs degrade in recovering features.
rows.note: No more specific Matryoshka outcome is stated for this setting.
rows.check: Only general degradation is reported; no absorption outcome is stated.

rows.subject: MP-SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic hierarchical data using residual-guided Matching Pursuit inference; evaluated learned features and activations.
rows.measure: Recovery of hierarchy, within-level correlations, and sparse-code support.
rows.baseline: Ground-truth dictionary and activation structure; ground-truth sparsity 1–2.
rows.value: Separates the hierarchy into four orthogonal sublevels of 1, 10, 3, and 6 features; learns an anchor direction and additional orthogonal directions within correlated ground-truth levels. It preserves conditional structure but reduces correlation and most inputs activate 2–4 components.
rows.note: Hierarchy is retained at the cost of matching the ground-truth correlations and support.
rows.check: Measures MP-SAE's split into orthogonal sublevels and its enlarged support, not parent–child absorption.

relation.reason: Its own results on absorption bear on V4 and V6.

tranche.reason: Results show a version is partial: MP-SAE removes absorption, and Matryoshka reduces it only inconsistently and with sibling distortion. B.1.4 also argues specifically that the original benchmark's perfectly correlated firing favours absorption. T5 fits better than T3.

source_check.notes: Within-level 'correlation' is similarity between same-level ground-truth directions, not firing co-occurrence. MP-SAE uses tied weights and no fixed l0 target; the others target 1.36. Sec 4.1 says Matryoshka avoids absorption, B.1.3 says only occasionally; Table 1: Matryoshka 0.048-0.22 vs Vanilla 0.45-0.70. Line 1203 has a leftover author edit note that is not addressed to an AI.

statements.problem: The study-specific sentence is accurate. Table 1 has Vanilla at 0.45-0.70 and BatchTopK at 0.42-0.54, in a separate child-distribution grid. Underestimation is stated explicitly only at correlation 0; at 0.3 the text says absorption 'remains'.
Faithful to appendix B.1.3. The Sec 4.1 main text says instead that Matryoshka 'avoids absorption' but adds sibling interference.
MP-SAE changes both the encoder and weight tying, and has no fixed l0 target (B.1.2). The heading covers both encoder and tying.

statements.correction: B.1.4 argues that fixed magnitudes (zp = lambda*zc) 'inherently favor' absorption. Table 1 varies child mean (0.1/0.5/1.0) and sd, with the parent fixed: Vanilla 0.45-0.70, BatchTopK 0.42-0.54, Matryoshka 0.048-0.22, MP-SAE 0.0011-0.073. At child mean 0.1 the child is not recovered (nan) except by MP-SAE. Vanilla's score is higher at mean 0.5 (0.70) than at mean 1.0 (0.45-0.47). Fig 16 (original benchmark, perfectly correlated firing): Vanilla consistently absorbs, Matryoshka avoids absorption with negative interference, MP-SAE is unstable.
statements.problem: Table 1 has no perfectly correlated condition. In B.1.4, 'favours absorption' is an argument, not a test. Standard SAEs absorb under every firing statistic tested, so the evidence does not show absorption is 'not universal'.

statements.correction: B.1.2: all SAEs except MP-SAE target l0 = 1.36. MP-SAE has no fixed target: it unrolls until the residual norm is below 0.05 or the support stabilizes. It also uses tied weights. Fig 16: under perfectly correlated firing, MP-SAE is unstable and only occasionally recovers parent-child pairs.
statements.problem: The fixed l0 target of 1.36 applies to Vanilla, BatchTopK and Matryoshka, not to MP-SAE, which this conflict is about.
Faithful to B.1.3 and Fig 16. Sec 4.1 main text says Matryoshka avoids absorption, and Table 1 Matryoshka scores (0.048-0.22) are well below Vanilla's.

statements.correction: B.1.3, correlation 0: in Vanilla and BatchTopK, child features align with their parents, and absorption makes parent activation values underestimated when a child is active. The active set is still identified correctly.
statements.problem: The study reports child features aligned with parents and parent activations underestimated, not a parent latent that goes silent ('clear parent holes').

statements.correction: B.1.3: 'Vanilla SAE and BatchTopK consistently exhibit feature absorption' across correlation levels. Correlation changes the recovery of within-level structure (Flat/Hierarchical MSE): Matryoshka struggles at 0.6, all degrade at 0.9, and at 0.9 MP-SAE splits levels into sublevels. Within-level correlation is similarity between same-level ground-truth directions, not firing co-occurrence. B.1.4 argues that perfect firing correlation favours absorption. Fig 16 shows Vanilla absorbing, Matryoshka avoiding absorption and MP-SAE unstable.
statements.problem: In an absorption-sensitivity line, this implies absorption changes with within-level correlation. The text says Vanilla and BatchTopK absorb consistently at every level. The perfect-correlation effect is the authors' argument.
Minor: the tree is adapted from the 2503.17547 benchmark, not the study's own. The changes are Gaussian firing magnitudes, mutually exclusive children and intra-level direction correlation.
True as stated. Note that within-level correlation is similarity between same-level dictionary directions, not firing co-occurrence; firing probabilities are fixed.
This study contributes objective dependence. Its correlation variable is within-level direction similarity, not parent-child co-occurrence.
